title: Poland Forges Ahead with U-20 Women's World Cup Despite UEFA's FIFA Boycott
summary: A bitter power struggle between global soccer's governing bodies is casting a shadow over the upcoming Under-20 Women's World Cup, but host nation Poland says the tournament will go on as planned. The competition, set for September 5–27, is the first FIFA event since UEFA's 55 member associations unanimously voted to boycott FIFA competitions. The boycott stems from FIFA President Gianni Infantino's controversial proposal—later abandoned—to sell 20% of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors for about $4.2 billion. UEFA has declared it has "lost confidence in Infantino's presidency" and insists conditions for ending the boycott have not been met. Despite the turmoil, the Polish Football Association (PZPN) said preparations are "in their final stage" and no team has indicated it will withdraw. "For many of these young players, this tournament represents an important milestone in their sporting careers," the PZPN stated. France was the first nation to confirm it will compete, followed by New Zealand, whose football spokesperson called the event "critical in the development for the women's game." The US is expected to participate but declined to comment, while England and Canada have remained silent. A source close to the discussions acknowledged that alternative tournaments might need to be considered if the dispute escalates, but added, "Those talks have not yet been had, and it is hoped they will not be necessary." Women's football is particularly vulnerable: the Under-17 Women's World Cup in Morocco this October and European qualifiers for the 2027 World Cup could also be affected. For now, though, the focus in Poland is on delivering a world-class event for the 24 competing teams.
why_it_matters: This conflict shows that decisions made in boardrooms far from the field can upend opportunities for young female athletes. If adults can't resolve the power struggle, a generation of players could lose crucial international experience, widening the gap between men's and women's soccer just as the women's game gains momentum.

background_read: FIFA (the worldwide governing body for soccer) and UEFA (the confederation representing European national associations) have a long history of tension, especially over money and control. Gianni Infantino became FIFA president in 2016 after a corruption scandal forced his predecessor out, promising reform. However, his push to sell a major stake in World Cup commercial rights to private investors alarmed European members, who saw it as reducing their influence and potentially diverting funds away from national associations. UEFA's unanimous boycott vote is an unprecedented act of defiance from its 55 members. Historically, UEFA has been a powerful bloc within FIFA, but this break threatens the structure of international soccer. The U-20 Women's World Cup is particularly important because youth tournaments give teenage players a rare global stage and often launch professional careers. If the boycott leads to canceled or weakened competitions, women's soccer—which already struggles for funding—could lose one of its key development platforms.

perspectives.description: For the 24 teams, especially those from smaller soccer nations, the tournament remains a priceless chance to compete at a world level and gain exposure. Poland, as host, can showcase its organizational capacity and boost local interest in women's soccer, which could leave a lasting legacy regardless of the political standoff.

The boycott creates a chaotic environment where players don't know if their tournament will go ahead as planned. Even if the event proceeds, the absence of major European powers or last-minute withdrawals could devalue the competition, and the dispute underscores how elite governance battles put grassroots athletes at risk.

The UEFA-FIFA split reflects deeper structural problems in global sports governance: who gets to control the money and decision-making? Infantino's commercial-rights plan was seen by UEFA as a power grab that would weaken national associations, while FIFA may view UEFA's boycott as an overreaction that hurts women's football for political gain. This is not the first power struggle, nor the last.

To protect youth tournaments, FIFA and UEFA may need a new compact that guarantees greater transparency and a say for national associations in commercial deals. If compromise fails, parallel tournaments might emerge, risking a split in the global game. Some argue that an independent body could oversee such competitions to keep them free of federation politics.
